summary: Chichikov, a gentleman of modest means, drives his britchka into a provincial Russian town and begins buying the names of dead serfs from the local landowners. Serfs are counted as souls in the property registers, and the dead ones still count until the next census. Each squire is a type: sentimental Manilov, the widow Korobochka, the bully Nozdrev, the miser Plyushkin. Gogol meant the book as a prose epic, the first part of three. The surviving second part breaks off, and the novel ends in mid-sentence.
context: Gogol published Dead Souls in Moscow in 1842. His friend Pushkin suggested the plot. He meant it as the Inferno of Russian life, with later parts showing Chichikov's regeneration. Shortly before his death in 1852 he burned the manuscript of the second part, and editors have rebuilt what survives from his notebooks. Many English versions followed, from Hapgood in 1886 to Hogarth in 1916. The site carries Hogarth's translation in the Standard Ebooks edition, with the translator's introduction.

people.name: Nikolai Gogol
people.note: Russian novelist of Ukrainian origin who lived from 1809 to 1852.

people.name: Pavel Ivanovich Chichikov
people.note: The traveller who buys dead serfs, and the book's picture of complacent vulgarity.

people.name: Alexander Pushkin
people.note: Gogol's friend, who suggested the plot.

people.name: Sobakevich
people.note: A strong, silent and economical squire.

people.name: Manilov
people.note: A sentimentalist among the landowners Chichikov visits.

people.name: Plyushkin
people.note: A miser who seems to rise above the book's vulgarity because he is miserable, not complacent.

people.name: C. J. Hogarth
people.note: Made the 1916 English translation that is now in the public domain.

ideas.title: Dead serfs as property
ideas.note: Serfs were counted as souls in registers, so dead ones still counted and could be traded or mortgaged.

ideas.title: Poshlost and vulgarity
ideas.note: The characters stand for different kinds of moral and spiritual commonplace.

ideas.title: Satire of Russian bureaucracy
ideas.note: The novel mocks the Russian middle aristocracy and the system around them.

ideas.title: A poem in prose
ideas.note: Gogol called it an epic poem in prose and planned it as a Divine Comedy of Russian life.

passages.quote: To the door of an inn in the provincial town of N. there drew up a smart britchka ⁠—a light spring-carriage of the sort affected by bachelors, retired lieutenant-colonels, staff-captains, landowners possessed of about a hundred souls, and, in short, all persons who rank as gentlemen of the intermediate category
passages.why: The opening scene of Chichikov's arrival.
